newsitem.title: ITALY: Scooter fans pay homage to Italy's Lambretta.
newsitem.headline: Scooter fans pay homage to Italy's Lambretta.

text.p: Fans from around the world paid homage to the Lambretta on Saturday, 50 years after the first scooter rolled off a production line in postwar Italy and became an icon for a style-conscious generation.

More than 1,000 Lambretta enthusiasts from Italy, England, Germany, the United States and even Japan rode, towed or trucked their beloved two-wheelers to the northern Italian city of Milan, where production first began in 1947.
To Britons growing up in the late 1950s and 'Swinging 60s', the Lambretta joined the miniskirt and "My Generation" music of The Who as symbols of 'Mod' youth culture.
Although the last Italian-built machine was sold 25 years ago and production ceased entirely in India in January this year, Lambretta lovers said the passion never died.
"We tried to drive all the way," said Philip Bush, 27, from Paisley in Scotland. "Unfortunately we couldn't get across the Swiss Alps because we were only doing about 15 miles an hour."
"We ended up hiring a van -- which was a shame but at least we got here," Bush said, standing next to his light blue Model B scooter which was built in 1949.

About 700 Lambrettas, the oldest dating from 1948, stood in a field on the outskirts of Milan waiting to take part in competitions organised by the Lambretta Club of Italy (LCI) as part of the anniversary.

Chrome handlebars gleamed in the sunlight as their owners lovingly polished the pastel-and-white paintwork or buffed wing mirrors ready for an acceleration test and a speed test -- where riders had to drive as slowly as possible.
The Lambretta was designed by Ferdinando Innocenti to meet the need for cheap transport in Italy after World War Two but quickly spread to other countries.
With its rival the Vespa, it put Italians on the road and opened new horizons for a generation emerging from the deprivations and suffering of war.
Among the high-pitched drone of engines and the smell of scooter fuel, there were plenty of owners sporting long, straight 1960s-style haircuts and sideburns.

Dave and Cath Cawley, both in their late 20s, rode all the way from Ashton-under-Lyne in northwest England on their immaculate 30-year-old white and chrome SX150 GP200. The journey took them more than four days.
For the Cawleys the passion for scooters stemmed from their youth.
"They're just stylish -- the style of when we were mods way back. You grow out of being a mod but you've still got the Lambretta," Cawley said.

Kazuhiro Nagasawa, 32, had come from Tokyo to fetch a newly restored 1951 Model B. Nagasawa, who was starting up a scooter club at home, said: "We have a passion for Italian scooters like Lambrettas and Vespas -- but we're not partisan like in Europe."
LCI chairman Vittorio Tessera said enthusiasts in Italy viewed the Lambretta as a closely-protected collector's item, unlike in England where people used theirs every day.
For Italians, the difference between a Lambretta and a Vespa stemmed from the postwar years when Vespas cost a little more and tended to have a better-heeled clientele.
"The Lambretta was more economic, simpler to work on and you always got a little dirtier," Tessera said.
The last Lambretta made, a modern black GP200 with the licence plate "Lam 200", was on display at the show.
Vic Dickens, 40, from London, was buffing up the lilac and white paintwork on his rare 30-year-old SX200 Special.
"A motorbike, they're all the same -- boring. But every scooter has got its own identity, you won't see one scooter the same," said Dickens.
